memo.thesis_en: I don't own Accenture, so the question is whether to start. On the numbers in front of me it looks cheap: roughly $252 a share against a conservative owner-earnings value of about $438, with five-year average ROE near 27% and debt-to-equity of 0.32. But a 43% discount on a business whose moat I can't verify is not a margin of safety, it's a question. Accenture sells people's time to clients, and the franchise rests on client relationships and the embedded nature of its work. I'm not at all sure AI and automation won't compress what clients pay for that labor over the next decade, and moats that must be rebuilt continuously are no moats at all. The snapshot also says nothing about ten years of earnings, ROIC, cash-flow quality or management, so I can't call the checklist complete. I'll put it on the watch list and wait until I can answer the durability question with confidence; waiting costs me nothing.

memo.thesis_en: I own this one, bought eleven days ago, and the return so far is a rounding error at 0.07%. That tells me nothing about the business, and I won't pretend otherwise. The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 29.3%, a reported debt-to-equity of 0.0, and owner earnings averaging about $646 million against a $6.0 billion market cap. The 67.9% margin of safety rests on an 8% growth rate and a 5% discount rate, and I distrust it. A metals fabricator sells something close to a commodity, so I'd mentally haircut that value hard, and I'd want to see a decade of earnings and the cash flow record before adding. No exit trigger is tripped: ROE is far above 15% and the price is nowhere near 1.5x intrinsic value. So I keep it, I don't add yet, and I keep asking whether the advantage is structural or just a good cycle.

memo.moat_analysis: My view is a modest low-cost and scale franchise in fabricated metal products, but the snapshot gives no cost, share or pricing data to prove it. The 29.3% five-year average ROE suggests above-average economics, though in a commodity-linked industry such returns can reflect a cycle rather than a structural moat. I give it a moderate durability estimate and would sell if ROE falls below the franchise test or cash flow turns negative.
memo.two_paragraph_business_description:
Mueller Industries manufactures fabricated metal products, principally copper-based tube, fittings and related industrial goods, sold into construction, HVAC, plumbing and industrial markets. The business is simple to describe: it buys metal, converts it into finished components, and earns a spread over raw material cost.

It makes money on volume, conversion margin and manufacturing and distribution efficiency, and the economics depend on cost position and discipline more than brand. The risk is that metal-linked businesses can look wonderful at the top of a cycle, so I treat the high ROE with respect but not blind faith.

memo.thesis_en: I can explain this business in two paragraphs: it builds warships for one dominant customer, the U.S. Navy, and there are very few places that customer can go. That is a regulatory-style moat, but a moat that comes from a single buyer's budget is not the same as a See's Candies brand, because the customer sets the terms. The snapshot shows a 45.7% margin of safety, but it rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, and I would want to haircut that for a shipbuilder with one customer. ROE of 15.26% and debt-to-equity of 0.49 only just clear my bars, with no cushion. The snapshot has no ten-year earnings record, no CEO tenure and no ROIC, so I cannot say the criteria are met. I don't own it, I have no pressing reason to buy it, and I will wait for the evidence.
memo.thesis_he: את העסק הזה אני יכול להסביר בשתי פסקאות: הוא בונה ספינות מלחמה ללקוח דומיננטי אחד, הצי האמריקאי, ויש מעט מאוד מקומות אחרים שהלקוח הזה יכול ללכת אליהם. זו חפיר מסוג רגולטורי, אבל חפיר שנשען על התקציב של קונה יחיד אינו מותג כמו See's Candies, כי הלקוח הוא זה שקובע את התנאים. מרווח הביטחון בנתונים עומד על 45.7%, אך הוא נשען על צמיחה של 8% ועל שיעור היוון של 5%, ואני רוצה להפחית ממנו כשמדובר בקבלן ביטחוני עם לקוח אחד. תשואה על ההון של 15.26% ויחס חוב להון של 0.49 בקושי עוברים את הרף שלי, בלי שום כרית. בנתונים אין היסטוריית רווחים של עשר שנים, אין כהונת מנכ"ל ואין ROIC, ולכן אינני יכול לומר שהקריטריונים התקיימו. אני לא מחזיק במניה, אין לי סיבה דחופה לקנות אותה, ואחכה לראיות.

memo.moat_analysis: The moat is regulatory and structural: building nuclear-capable and large surface warships takes specialized yards, a skilled workforce, security clearances and decades of Navy relationships, and few rivals could enter. The weakness is that the Navy is both the sole customer and the price-setter, so the pricing power I demand from a true franchise is limited. Fixed-price contract risk and dependence on congressional appropriations can erode economics even where competition is absent. The snapshot's 5-year average ROE of 15.26% is consistent with a decent but not exceptional franchise, and it only barely clears my threshold.
memo.two_paragraph_business_description:
Huntington Ingalls is a U.S. naval shipbuilder. It designs, builds, overhauls and maintains large warships and submarines, chiefly for the U.S. Navy and Coast Guard, and it also provides related technical and mission services. Its yards are among the few in the country able to build the largest and most complex vessels, which limits competition.

It earns money through long-term government contracts, which pay either a cost-plus fee or a fixed price. Revenue is therefore tied to the Navy's shipbuilding budget and to how well the company controls costs, labor and schedule. Returns come from steady, lumpy program execution rather than from consumer pricing power, which is why I treat the moat as real but not unlimited.
